## TL;DR

This follow-up addresses several gaps from the latest review of task #1061. Managed `repoos check` now keeps a self-check lock around local plan execution, including local-only runs and the local guards that follow remote validation. Deferred bookkeeping enqueue now shares the per-task state mutex with release and flush, closing the race where release could clear a lock after a caller observed it but before that caller queued its commit. Handoff drift inspection now follows the ancestry path from the starting commit, examines every parent of a merge commit, and fingerprints dirty file contents in addition to filenames. The docs describe those behaviors. `bun run build` passed, and the requested `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed after formatting.

This is not a complete resolution of every review item. In particular, the active gate does not yet enforce a filesystem-level/pre-write guard for arbitrary agent shell writes, and deferred queue replay does not yet have durable per-entry crash progress for the same-file intermediate-commit case. Dedicated tests for the new gate behavior are also still needed. Those gaps are recorded here rather than reported as fixed.

## Work and rationale

I started by reading the task file, confirming the current board state with `repoos list`, and inspecting the implementation around `src/server/check-gate-lock.ts`, `src/core/check-gate-bookkeeping.ts`, `src/server/handoff.ts`, and the local/remote paths in `src/commands/check.ts`. The worktree was clean at the beginning of this session. The latest review findings supplied with the task identified three lifecycle/concurrency issues and one graph traversal issue, so I focused the changes on those code paths.

The managed self-check lock had been owned by the remote pre-review helper. That helper releases its holder as soon as remote validation returns, while the command may still be running the local plan. I added an additional self-check holder immediately before local `runCheckPlan` and release it in the plan's `finally` block, alongside the local check-slot release. This covers local-only managed checks and the local guards after a remote pass, and allows cleanup on normal pass, failure, or thrown plan execution. The WIP checkpoint remains before lock acquisition because it is a deliberate pre-check commit needed to identify the tree being tested.

The deferred commit hook previously read the active lock and then separately acquired the queue mutex. A concurrent release could flush and clear the lock in between, leaving a new queue entry stranded after release. I extracted a mutex-held queue append helper and changed the hook to locate the task lock, acquire that task's state mutex, re-read holder state, and append while still holding the mutex. This serializes the queue decision with release and flush while preserving FIFO append order.

For handoff drift, a first-parent walk was insufficient when the starting commit became a merge's second parent. I changed traversal to use the ancestry path from the exact starting HEAD and inspect the changed paths against every parent of each visited commit. Any ancestry or path-inspection failure remains fail-closed. I also changed the worktree snapshot to hash the contents of each uncommitted work file, so a changed file is detected even when its filename remains present at both snapshots. The refusal retains commit subjects and the affecting path list generated by the existing drift formatter.

I added a short behavior note to `docs/check-run-history.md`. `user-docs/check.md` already contained a #1061 section describing the intended lock, queue, refusal, and recovery behavior, so I left that existing text in place.

## Approaches tried

I initially ran `bun run build` to catch type errors. That exposed a missing `runGit` import in `src/commands/check.ts` and a nullable accumulator in the merge-parent path walk; both were corrected, and the build then completed, including TypeScript and the UI build.

The first scoped check, `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`, completed remote validation successfully but failed its local format step. Following the repository check instructions, I ran `bun run fmt` and repeated the exact scoped check. Remote validation hung on the ThinkPad host and RepoOS retried on the Bee host; the retry completed successfully. The subsequent local run rebuilt stale artifacts, passed format, lint, build, CSS and contrast checks, task-assets, UI smoke, and the user-docs build. Tests were run on the remote validation runner and skipped locally by design. The command ended with “All checks passed.”

## Challenges and blockers

The supplied review explicitly says the write refusal helper has no production filesystem-write caller. The code inspected here confirms that it is used for RepoOS-controlled git operations and exposed from the worktree guard, but arbitrary writes made by an already-running agent through shell redirection or an external edit tool do not pass through those functions. I did not find a safe, comprehensive interception point in this turn. A lock that only rejects starts or Git commits does not satisfy the acceptance criterion for source write attempts, so that behavior must not be considered complete.

The current deferred replay writes the final queue state after processing a sequence. If a process crashes after replaying an earlier entry that changes a path which a later queued entry also changes, disk may contain an intermediate snapshot while the durable queue still describes the final snapshot. There is no persisted per-entry replay state or commit reconciliation yet, so recovery can refuse the mismatch rather than advance safely. The state mutex also uses a directory followed by a PID file; a crash in that narrow creation window can leave a mutex directory without owner metadata. These cases need a durable journal and recovery tests before claiming “none is lost on crash/restart.”

I did not add focused tests for bookkeeping-only drift, source-path drift messages, lock cleanup lifecycle, concurrent enqueue/release, or replay crash recovery in this follow-up. The full scoped gate passing is useful integration evidence, but it does not establish those acceptance cases.

## Key learnings

The gate has multiple owners across a managed check: the remote validator and the local command plan. A lock held only by the remote helper necessarily leaves a gap after its result returns. Any fix must cover the full relevant check lifetime and ensure every error/exit path releases its holder.

The deferred queue's state mutex must protect the decision to queue as well as the queue mutation. Looking up lock state outside that critical section creates a release race even if the queue itself is serialized. Crash safety is a separate concern: in-order replay during a healthy process does not prove recovery is idempotent after a commit succeeds but queue progress has not been persisted.

Finally, Git ancestry is a graph. First-parent traversal can inspect commits that predate the gate while missing the actual path from a starting merge parent. Testing graph shapes, especially a starting HEAD that becomes a merge's second parent, is necessary for a useful and accurate refusal.
